title: Genjokoan 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett explores Dogen's Genjokoans as a way to live fully present in life, acknowledging that our individual perspectives are inherently incomplete and limited. By embracing this realization, we can approach reality with openness and awareness, rather than trying to change or improve it through thinking. This approach encourages us to focus on the immediate present moment, letting go of assumptions and striving for enlightenment, and instead cultivating a sense of wonder and appreciation for life's complexities.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
Old friends and new friends, thanks for being here.
Hi, Les.
Nice to see you.
Friends from Hawaii.
Well, it was a little challenging for me preparing for this retreat.

I want to admit up front, so I can get it out of the way, that we went through a whole process, four of us working with Norman Fischer, our teacher: a year of training and preparation for dharma transmission, where you receive the brown robe and then you're graduated or something.
Most of it was very organic and sweet and lovely and felt as a life step should.
You're a little unsure, but it feels natural.
You know what I mean?
You just take the step and it's okay.
You're not quite ready, but you're ready enough.
But the one aspect of all this that for some reason was stuck in my craw was leading this particular retreat.
I was just really nervous about it.
This weekend study retreat is something we asked Norman to do starting maybe 10 or 12 years ago.
We noticed in our schedule that we already had a weekly sitting group, and we were doing meditation and starting to add meditation retreats.
That seemed to be going okay, but part of our being in the boonies in a certain way was that there were not so many teachers around then, 10, 12, 15 years ago.
We thought it would really help us to have a time once a year where we really focus on study, like a seminar or a class in Dharma studies and Zen studies.
So we asked Norman to do that, and we more or less invented this format of a weekend retreat that's half a meditation retreat and half a class or a seminar.
Since we more or less invented it, and we only ever saw Norman leading it, I felt more in my consciousness, well, this is really Norman's thing.
How can you sit in that seat?
At the same time, as it goes when you're nervous about something, part of you recognizes that it's actually okay.
You recognize that it's just a thought, and it's compelling, and it keeps convincing me.
It's like talking to me in the back of my head.
Do you have thoughts like that?
You're not good enough.
You're not good enough.
You say hello.

Anyway, it does feel like big shoes to fill, and then just to up the ante, I was very busy with work for the last month and lots of things were going on, so I didn't feel like I had much time to prepare.
But today I feel okay.
So maybe it'll be okay.
I want to mention to the people who are attending the retreat that we recognize we swung or sprung dokusan on you, private interviews.
This is part of evolving this retreat.
When Norman was leading it, we would have 40 people or more.
We would not use the Saturday evening for zazen, which can also have interviews, so there was less time.
We'd do other things on the Saturday evening with him.
Now we have fewer people and we're using the Saturday evening for meditation.
I hope you noticed; we're asking you to come back in the evening.
And so it's possible to do dokusan, so we decided to go ahead and do it.
But it's also a treasured and important part of Zen training, one that we don't access too often, to pull the rug out from everybody once in a while and do something different or change the schedule.
We're so conditioned that our comfort with things to some extent revolves around being able to anticipate the future.
Have you noticed that?
We want to know what's coming next and we want to be comfortable with that.
We want to have done it before.
Despite all of our talk about beginner's mind, we actually want to be experts at all times.
So it's actually useful to show up at a retreat or some situation, think it's going to go one way, and then it goes another way.
Somebody came to see me and said, "But I didn't prepare anything," which is great.
That's great.
So don't, [unclear: "a kid will invite you"] and it's an invitation too.
You don't have to come if you choose not to.
It's fine.
But if you do come, you don't have to be prepared.
We'll just talk a minute.
So part of my nervousness, since I was nervous about this retreat, was that it was really hard for me to pick a topic, because that would be acknowledging that I was actually going to do it.
It's interesting to notice these little ways that we avoid things.
Indecisiveness is one.

But luckily, our colleagues in the North, Myoshin Kate McCandless and Shinwon Michael Newton and the Sangha there in Vancouver, are having a practice period right now, and I understand Seattle [unclear: "Zoroastrianism"] is also having a practice period right now.
It's wonderful.
The topic of the practice period in Vancouver is life koans, life koans.
We could have a whole lecture on what that means, a koan, but it's some sort of story or question about something.
So, life koans.
Kate suggested that I take up as a topic for this retreat Dogen's Genjokoans, so the people from Vancouver, and there are a few folks here from Vancouver, can add this study.
Of Norman's, or Dogen's, funny Freudian slip, a Dogenian slip.
Dogen's essay Genjokoan, which is essentially his explication of life koans.
The koan is the question of what it means to really show up in our life.
Kate thought it was kind of cute.
I was nervous because our dynamic is that she's the one who's nervous and I'm the one who's overconfident, so we switched roles.
She was laughing at me and saying, "Why don't you do Genjokoan?"
I said, "Oh, thank you."
So now I'm okay.
We can talk about Genjokoan.
So who was Dogen?
Who was Eihei Dogen?
And why would he matter to us now?
Why should we study this?
There are lots of things we can study, lots of things we could do with our Saturday.
A few of the facts of the matter are that Dogen was a 13th century Japanese man with a strong religious orientation and practice, and we'll talk more about his life later.
He's credited now with bringing some sense of Zen practice from China to Japan in about 1225, 1226, after going himself to China as a young man for a few years.
He's an unusual Zen master because he wrote a lot.
He wrote a lot: essays, lectures, letters, all kinds of things.
Somehow his writings mostly survive to the present day.
One of his famous writings is this short essay, and did you get a little pamphlet?
It's very short.
I could give you a little three-page handout.
There's a three-page handout of the essay, and there's a two-page handout of dozens of big, thick, expensive books you can buy to try to understand the essay.
You're welcome to take that with you, even if you're just here visiting for the talk.
Dogen, from the beginning, was interested in this question: how do we live?
What does it mean to really be fully alive?
In the traditional biographies of him, they say that when his mother died, when he was a child, seven years old, at the funeral they offered incense,
and the seven-year-old boy, looking at the incense smoke, was of course sad and confused like any child would be at the funeral of their parent, but some other sense arose, they say.
Some sense of: how can this be?
This is the great religious question.
How can this be, that we live and die like smoke?
He went off.
He ordained as a monk as a young man, 13 years old.
One of the teachings he was told at the Tendai Buddhist monastery was that we're all Buddhas.
We're all expressing some pure, awakened essence of life.
And he wondered, they say, but why am I so confused?
That's true, and it seems like maybe it is.
There's some feeling to that.
Why do we have to do all this?
Why do we have to practice?
Why do we have to study?
Why do we have to develop and think and meditate and do all these things?
In that school of Buddhism there are many complicated rituals to learn.
How does this all work?
I think we have the same question even if we don't frame it in that way.
There's some sense that it's okay to be who we are.
There's some sense of that, and also some strong sense of the opposite.
We have to fix, we have to improve, we have to learn, we have to study, we have to develop, we have to mature, we have to grow up.
How do these two things work together?
The traditional story was that that was his question, and he spent the rest of his life investigating it.

As we talk a little over the weekend about Dogen's biography, I'll bring up a fun twist for us doing Dogen studies in the present day: scholars now doubt that the majority of the traditional stories are actually historically true.
That's fun too.
We'll talk about that.
What does it mean for something to be true?
Dogen also did an unusual kind of writing for a Zen teacher.
Mostly Zen teachers' writings were very short, pithy, dense maybe, mostly connected to the stories of earlier Zen teachers, a sense of carrying something forward.
Dogen's writing has a quality of that, but he also did some unusually discursive essays where he explored metaphors and poetic images.

In many ways he was referencing earlier Chinese Zen stories, but turning them around and looking at them in different ways, writing longer essays and giving these as longer talks than was traditionally the case.
What we think of now as a Dharma talk was not actually done in 11th and 12th century China.
The way a Dharma talk was done, the teacher would enter the room and step up on a raised platform, and you would all be standing.
This was done in the middle of the day.
The talk was about five or ten minutes long and probably didn't make any sense to you in the usual way of something making sense.
And that's it.
This was a Dharma talk, and I can read you one later in the retreat.
Dogen also did that kind of Dharma talk, and they collected those in a different book, which has only recently been translated into English.
But Zen teachers also sometimes did informal talks, often late at night.
One of the talks in this category, collected, recorded by [unclear: "Domen"], he proudly writes in the little colophon, was given at two in the morning.
A long, complicated, discursive, poetic talk.
Two in the morning.
Our text for the weekend is in that category of an informal talk, probably given at night, which Dogen gave more of and wrote down, both of which were unusual.
These collected essays and talks, these informal, discursive talks, were later collected into a book.
But we really don't know if that was Dogen's intention at the time.
There are many powerful teachings for us in this short, three-page text.
For this opening talk, I'll give just a few examples and a little more explication of the background and where we're doing this.
Then for those of us staying in the retreat, we'll work our way through the whole text in the next three talks.
So I'm not even going in order.
You don't even need your handouts yet.
I'm just going to jump around a little for this first talk and try to set the stage.
If you're not able to stay for the retreat, you'll have the handout, and we'll also put the recordings of the other talks on the website if you want to continue your study of Genjokoan.
Here's a line from Genjokoan.
*When you see forms or hear sounds, fully engaging body and mind, you intuit Dharma immediately.*
*When you see forms and hear sounds, fully engaging body and mind, you intuit Dharma immediately.*
Oh, yes, intimately.
Thank you very much.
I'm misreading my word here.
Intimately.
So this is not right away what we think of as spiritual practice: something about seeing and hearing, something about intimacy.
Thank you, Bob.
And body and mind.
I think sometimes we think about personal development or spiritual work as a mind process.
So, body and mind.
If we think about this, we realize that this world we think we're in is really based on what the senses bring in.
This process happens so constantly we don't always think about it.
So what are you seeing right now?
What are you hearing right now?
This is only happening right now, so there's a returning here to the immediacy of experience.
The whole world, just this opening of the senses.
And yet Dogen seems to be saying there's something deeply true about just being aware of something, according to our complicated mind, as simple as seeing and hearing.
But he also talks in our text about some limitations to perception and cognition.
Another place in the text he says,
*unlike things and their reflections in the mirror, and unlike the moon and its reflection in the water, when one side is illuminated, the other side is dark.*
*Unlike things and their reflections in the mirror, and unlike the moon and its reflection in the water, when one side is illuminated, the other side is dark.*
So, one side.
There's a certain way that we can see one side of something and forget that we're not seeing the other side.
So we see one side and we think we see the whole thing.
And is our life just reflecting something we're seeing?
Or is there something else going on?
He says it's another way with the metaphor about being in a little boat in the ocean.
Something he experienced himself as a young man when he took this journey to China, which was apparently a somewhat dangerous voyage to take, and it took several weeks.
Pretty small boat, I bet.
He writes in another place in Genjokoan:

*When you sail out in a boat to the middle of the ocean and there's no land in sight, or no land is in sight, and view the four directions, the ocean looks circular and does not look any other way, but the ocean is neither round nor square.
Its features are infinite in variety.
It is like a palace.
It is like a jewel.
It only looks circular as far as you can see at that time.
All things are like this.
While there are many features in the dusty world and the world beyond conditions, you see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.*
Tell me about the shape of our world.

*When you sail out in a boat in the middle of the ocean, there's no land in sight, and view the four directions, the ocean looks circular and does not look any other way.* See, right in the middle of the water.
*The ocean is neither round nor square.
Its features are infinite in variety.
It is like a palace.
It is like a jewel.
It only looks circular as far as you can see at that time.
All things are like this.

Although there are many features in the dusty world and the world beyond conditions, you see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.* So there's something inherently incomplete about our view of the world.
And yet we act as if we know the world.
And in many ways our view is a bit discouraged, isn't it, of the world?
It seems like we live in a time when the world is really in trouble.
It's really burning.
There are wars always going on.
The climate is changing.
Species are being lost.
We hold that view.
Maybe we don't try to think about it, but we might hold that view.
But do we really know the shape of the world?
Do we really know what's going on?
There was a just published book by a cognitive scientist named Steven Pinker.
He's a cognitive psychologist at Harvard.
The book is called The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined.
The Better Angels of Our Nature, Why Violence Has Declined.
I've not read this book.
I read a long book review.
It's like an 800-page book on this topic.
Why has violence declined?
And in the book, according to the review, he makes a strong case that actually this is the least violent and the safest time in human history, which is surprising to us.

He says in the book, if you really look at all the evidence and statistics that are available to us, the scientific facts on the ground, death from war and murder in particular is at an all-time low relative to the human population of the earth.
In terms of your probability of being killed in a murder or a war, this is the best time ever.
Of course, there are plenty of impressive and horrible wars and genocides going on, but compared to earlier times, things are really, really good.
And the further good news that he posits is that it's not just good luck.
There's actually a long positive cultural change that's been going on over the centuries.
That as a whole, as a human culture, we are more positive, more moral.
That we don't approve of things like slavery and torture and cruel punishment in a way that all this was taken for granted in previous centuries.
So the review of his arguments was pretty impressive, and I thought, huh, I have this view that it's really a terrible time in the world.
So which is it?
The world is burning, and it's also more peaceful than ever.
In a lot of ways, it's useful, I think, to explore and study Dogen.
His writings really encourage us not to be stuck on one side or the other.
And because of this, studying Dogen is a little bit confusing in a sort of conventional way of reading.
And you read some of the commentaries on Genjokoan, and especially the ones by scholars, they all say, this is a very difficult text.
And it is difficult in a certain way.
But so is getting out of bed in the morning.
Right?
So that's our eye of practice again.
Do we see this as difficult, something that we need to understand and process and sort of conceptualize in a certain way?
Or is it something else?
And Dogen was encouraging us not to hold either view, I think.
My preparation for the seminar was I listened to a bunch of talks Norman gave, I have to admit.
A whole series of talks were recorded in Switzerland, actually.
Iris was there, so it was fun to think about her sitting there.
And he gave like a seven-day retreat on this text.
So there's more time for meditation and just sort of processing it all.
And the thing I was impressed about his series of talks about Genjokoan was, I went into this as anyone would, thinking, oh good, I found this series of six talks, it's like six hours.
And it was sure to help me understand this text so that I can say something.
Sure to work.
But the thing that impressed me was not how well he explained the text, but actually how little he explained.
And in one of his talks he reads a whole other Dogen text about enlightenment, which I won't trouble you with.
Sort of a long excerpt of another essay about enlightenment, an essay called The Great Enlightenment, which is very confusing.
And Norman read this and said, well maybe Dogen wants us to be a little less sure that we know what enlightenment is, what confusion is.
Maybe this is, kind of, it's okay to be a little off balance.
If we have some grounding and some support so that our off-balanceness can be [unclear: "consolated"] in humility, in openness, and actually even in joy.
So maybe this is again our beginner's mind.
So another famous passage in Genjokoan that I've been thinking about a lot lately, and I've mentioned it a few times here, is this:
*To carry the self forward and illuminate myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forward and illuminate the self is awakening.*
So, *to carry the self forward and illuminate myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and illuminate the self is awakening.*
So here we have the self entering the story.
The self was implied in our last few quotes, but here is the self directly.
What is the self that we're carrying around, or that is carrying us around?
With all of its views and opinions, all of the things it thinks it does understand or doesn't understand, all of its definition and tendencies and habits, I'm such-and-so kind of person.
The self that we're carrying forward to meet the world.
So myriad things means the world.
And is that carrying forward the only way to go, or is there also some possibility that we don't have to do that so much?
That the world will come forth and help us without our intervention and tinkering.
Is that another possibility?
But when we first read such a passage, "to carry the self forward and illuminate the myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and illuminate the self is awakening," we right away think, oh good, it's going to tell us what to do.
So I'll have a better self.
I actually don't think he means that it's not a good idea to carry yourself forward, and that it is a good idea to just sit in deep samadhi and let the world come to you.
How do we add that value of judgment when we hear such a teaching?
It's more saying both these things are always in play.
But can you recognize that?
Can you see what's happening a little more clearly?
So Zen, partly how it came to us in the West, came with a certain sort of reputation, a certain sort of rep.
A sort of powerful, philosophical, cutting-through thing.
A cool and hip thing, for sure.
Which is strange, because it's mostly not very cool people who are into practicing Zen.
I guess we're the ones who stuck around.
The cool people aren't just happily doing their cool thing.
But actually Zen is a school of Buddhism.
So Zen is not fundamentally interested in philosophy or being cool or some certain sort of glow.
It's actually interested in liberation, which is a fancy way really of saying it's interested in happiness.
It's interested in happiness.
In contentment, in peacefulness.
And so we started out with not only the hip and cool stuff to get us there, but we also started out with the great enlightenment.
With this powerful idea that there's some other version of us, which is the awakened us that we'll get later if we try really hard on our cushions.
And this is back to Dogen's question again.
Are we already okay the way we are?
Or do we need some improvement?
Or both?
Or neither?
But at its root, Buddhism is interested in how there could be less stress and suffering in your life.
And how that might make it possible to be kinder and more connected to others, so that the whole world could have less stress and suffering.
And so we're reading Dogen 50 or 60 years into the experiment of American Zen.
And it's a wonderful time, when some ideas are shifting and hopefully rebalancing in a certain way.
Probably 50 years from now they'll say, oh, back then they didn't really understand this, but by now we feel good.

We can not only be free from suffering, but free from the additional suffering of trying to use our practice to change us into some other person whom we are not, which is a very pernicious kind of suffering.
And you meet people who are really caught in the thralls of that.
They're really miserable.
They could be excellent meditators, but they could be really miserable.
I remember one time we had a visiting Zen teacher here to help us, actually to help us do some sewing.
We do the different ordination steps.
We sew our own robes, a great thing.
And we had set up the room like a sewing room, so it didn't really look like a meditation hall.
There were tables and equipment and stuff.
So it was a Dharma hall or two ago.
And we wanted to sit a little bit of meditation, informally, in a circle in the middle before we started sewing.
And I remember the visiting teacher asked me, as we were about to sit down, well, would you face in or face out?
I think she just wanted to do it the consistent way that we do things.
And we mostly sit facing out, towards the walls.
That's part of our tradition, facing towards the wall.
Different groups do it differently.
But I was looking around at this cluttered room and thinking, well, maybe this is a little different situation.
Let's face in.
And so I said to her, well, maybe sitting in might be friendlier.
And she looked at me quite askance, actually, and said very emphatically to me, "Zazen has nothing to do with friendliness."
And this is a teacher I love and respect very much, not just some wacky sewing teacher that we met at the corner.
But there's a certain attitude that came to us earlier in the Zen movement.
I'm curious what she would say now.
In a way, that's really true.
Zazen is, in some way, meditation is in some way about an exploration that is deeper than being friendly or being unfriendly, or me being friendly or me being unfriendly.
But actually, I think Zazen is about nothing but friendliness.
It's a deeper kind of friendliness than a friendliness that's based on a self trying to negotiate its self-worth or be validated or something.
It's a kind of friendliness with experience itself.
And that's what Genjokoan is talking about.
Is it possibly more deeply friendly with our experience the way it is?
And as we study this point, or even sit meditation for about a minute and a half, we notice thinking.
We notice thinking.
And we notice how thinking so powerfully creates our world.
And again, this is like that first quote.
We see and we hear.
And then very quickly we think, I know what that is.
In some ways, our thinking can be even a sort of math that occludes perception.
Because we think we know what it is, we don't actually look.
We don't actually hear.
And once we think, we have a position or a view.
How things should be, how they shouldn't be.
And that's part of the great joy of Sangha life.
We bump into each other a little bit because we have all these views, how things are supposed to go here.
We had a little discussion the other night, a warm-up to the retreat.
I was saying the other night, what's great about religion is we take it very seriously.
We have very strong ideas about how it's supposed to be, based on a deep tradition and all this.
But actually, it's all made up.
And so we can see in that context, the background is a made-up religion that came from some other culture anyway.
You know, what are we doing?
Sometimes, not always, it's possible to say, "Oh, that's just a view.
Here I am, so upset, so worked up, so concerned, sending many emails and convening many meetings because of this view."
And that might be why Dogen can be a little hard to read.
He can bring up one view very strongly and bring up the opposite view very strongly.

He'll make a strong argument for A, and a strong argument for B, and a strong argument for not A, and a strong argument for not B, and a strong argument for A and B, and a strong argument for not A and not B.
I'm not sure what else there is, but there's probably a few more.
So he's building on a sort of dialectic around an understanding of reality.
What is the reality that's beyond the ways that we put things into categories?
Sometimes we use the word emptiness for this.
But as we study our thinking and our views, we really can see how powerfully we create our world with our thinking.
Because we externalize reality so strongly, we think if we could just improve the external reality, we would be happier.
And that may be true.
But it might be that our internal constructed reality is much more powerful and much more profound and much more important.
So I've been meaning for a very long time to read Victor Frankl's *Man's Search for Meaning*.
Did you read that book, maybe long ago?
If you haven't, Victor Frankl was a concentration camp survivor.
It's back to the earlier point about being a safer era.
Fifty-five million people died during World War II.
I forget, ten or eleven, twelve million died in the concentration camps.
Victor Frankl lived through most of the war in the camps.
Very few people did.
He was, I think, a medical doctor going into it, but he ended up becoming a psychologist.
I might have that a little backwards.

After he survived the war and survived liberation from the camps, which is one of the things he added to the field of psychology, he looked at the psychology of what happens after you're freed from a terrible situation.
He previously thought, okay, you're good now.
It's more complicated than that.
But anyway, he also survived the aftermath of the camps, which not all of the prisoners did.
He didn't frame it the way Dogen would have, but in extreme circumstances he learned something about the power of this world constructed with thinking.
He framed it in terms of the future.
We would frame it maybe more in terms of the present.
So, a few things from Victor Frankl.
There was a lot of setup, and I won't read you all of it.

He talks about how horrible and difficult it is: a tiny amount of food, working very long days in the cold with very little clothing, random acts of cruelty and kindness in the camps, and people dying all the time.
And actually, the image that stuck with me most powerfully from the earlier part of the book, I'll just mention that, and then I'll read you these excerpts.
When they arrived at the camp, they started at Auschwitz, and then they got moved to Dachau, I think.
Anyway, they arrived at the camp after being crammed into these cattle cars.
We all kind of know this story.
They're walking off, being herded along, and then there's an SS official standing there.
He's just gesturing like this, Victor Frankl explains: gesturing to the left, gesturing to the right.
Of course, none of them knew what was going on.
Really extreme.
They'd been trained in that way.
They didn't know what was going on.
But he found out later that the gesture to the left meant immediate execution, and the gesture to the right meant you look like you're worth keeping as a worker.
So he got sent to the right.
So he writes, thank you, Cooks.
Yeah, you can listen to the recording later.
*The prisoner who has lost faith in the future, his future, was doomed.
With his loss of belief in the future, he also lost his spiritual hold.
He let himself decline and became subject to mental and physical decay.
Usually this happened quite suddenly in the form of a crisis.
The symptoms of which were familiar to the experienced camp inmate.
We all feared this moment.
Not for ourselves, which would have been pointless, but for our friends.
Usually it began with the prisoner refusing one morning to get dressed or washed or go out under the parade grounds.
And no entreaties or blows or threats had any effect.
He just lay there, hardly moving.
If this crisis was brought about by an illness, he refused to be taken to the sick bay or to do anything to help himself.
He simply gave up.
And there he remained, lying in his own excreta and nothing bothered him anymore.*
*I once had a dramatic demonstration of the close link between loss of faith in the future and this dangerous giving up.
F, my senior block warden and a fairly well-known composer and librettist confided in me one day.
"I would like to tell you something, Doctor.
I've had a strange dream.
I've always told me I could wish for anything and that I should only say what I most wanted to know and that my question would be answered.
Do you know what I asked?
I asked that I would like to know when the war would be over for me.
You know what I mean, Doctor, for me.
I wanted to know when our camp would be liberated and our sufferings would come to an end."
"And when did you have this dream?"
I asked.
"In February, 1945," he answered.
It was then the beginning of March.
"And did your dream answer?"
I asked him.
Furtively, he whispered to me, "March 30th."*
*When F told me about his dream, he was still full of hope and convinced that the voice of his dream would be right.
But as the promised day grew nearer, the war news which reached our camp made it appear unlikely that he would be free by this promised date.
And on March 29th, F suddenly became ill and read a high temperature.
And on March 30th, the day his prophecy had told him that the war and his suffering would be over for him, he became delirious and lost consciousness.
And on March 31st, he was dead.
To outward appearances, he had died of typhus.
But I did not think that is why he died.*
That's from Viktor Frankl.
So the external circumstances hadn't really changed there.
Something changed in thinking.
Let's see.
